                                              AN ORDER AUTOMORPHISM OF A DLAB GROUP NOT INDUCED BY
                                                                  CONJUGATION

                                                                 TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


                                                  Abstract. Let G = D⟨2⟩ ([0, 1]) be equipped with either of its two Dlab orders. There exists
                                                  an order automorphism α of G such that, for every rank-one subgroup H ≤ R×    >0 , every one of
                                                  the six corresponding Dlab groups A listed below, equipped with any of its linear orders, every




arXiv:2609.18630v1 [math.GR] 16 Sep 2026
                                                  order-preserving embedding e : G ,→ A, and every u ∈ A, there exists f ∈ G such that e(α(f )) ̸=
                                                  u−1 e(f )u.




                                                                                       1. Introduction
                                              An order automorphism of an ordered group is an automorphism preserving its specified linear
                                           order. Kopytov and Medvedev posed Problem 21.149 in the Kourovka Notebook ; in its original
                                           form, the problem asks whether a Dlab group can have an order automorphism that is not inner
                                           [2]. Van Doorn, Judin, Monticone and Morrison report that they obtained an affirmative solution
                                           to this original formulation and sent it to the editors of the Kourovka Notebook. According to their
                                           account, one of the problem authors checked the solution and agreed that it was correct, but then
                                           explained that the intended question was stronger: whether there exists an order automorphism of
                                           a Dlab group that is not induced by conjugation by an element of a possibly larger Dlab group [4,
                                           Appendix A]. They further state that the problem statement was revised to reflect this intended
                                           meaning and that the stronger problem remained open. Thus the distinction is essential: an
                                           automorphism may be non-inner in the original Dlab group but still be induced by conjugation
                                           after that group is embedded in a larger Dlab group. The theorem below addresses this clarified
                                           form of Problem 21.149 for the six rank-one Dlab groups considered here.
                                              Put
                                                                                I = [0, 1],     G = D⟨2⟩ (I).
                                           For a homeomorphism g, write supp(g) = {x : g(x) ̸= x}. A support component of g is a component
                                           of supp(g). The group G has two Dlab orders, described in Section 2. We equip G with either one
                                           of them and fix that choice throughout.
                                              If a group B acts by increasing homeomorphisms on an interval, write Fix(B) for its common
                                           fixed-point set and call a component of the complement of Fix(B) an action component of B. By
                                           the standard action of G we mean its defining action on (0, 1).
                                              We use the notation for the six larger groups from [3]. On I, DH (I) consists of the elements
                                           that are the identity near both endpoints, DH∗ (I) of those that are the identity near 0, D∗H (I) of
                                           those that are the identity near 1, and DH (I) is the full interval group. On R, DH consists of the
                                           elements with bounded support and DH∗ of those whose support is bounded below.
                                              We construct an increasing homeomorphism h of [0, 1] which has finitely many affine pieces, all
                                           with slopes in ⟨2⟩, on every compact subinterval of (0, 1]. The support components of h form a
                                           strictly descending sequence toward 0. Conjugation by h normalizes G and preserves its order.
                                           By contrast, for each element of the six larger Dlab groups considered here, the components of its
                                           support are well ordered from left to right.
                                              2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. 06F15, 20F60, 20E36.
                                              Key words and phrases. ordered group, Dlab group, order automorphism, piecewise linear homeomorphism,
                                           conjugation.
                                                                                                 1
2                        TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


   For an arbitrary order-preserving embedding e : G ,→ A, we study the components of the
complement of the common fixed-point set of e(G). They have a least member, denoted later by J0 .
Subgroups supported on disjoint source intervals commute, and their least nontrivial components
inside J0 are disjoint and occur in the same order as the source intervals. The resulting nested
intervals determine the points of (0, 1) and yield a conjugacy between the standard action of G and
the action of e(G) on J0 .
   The main result is the following.
Theorem 1.1. Equip G = D⟨2⟩ (I) with either of its two Dlab orders. There is an order automor-
phism α of G such that, for every rank-one subgroup H ≤ R×     >0 , every one of the six corresponding
Dlab groups A listed below, equipped with any of its linear orders, every order-preserving embedding
e : G ,→ A, and every u ∈ A, there exists f ∈ G for which
                                         e(α(f )) ̸= u−1 e(f )u.
Here A may be any of the following six groups
                       DH (I),    DH∗ (I),    D∗H (I),   DH (I),    DH ,   DH∗ .
   The theorem is restricted to the six rank-one groups listed in [3]. Zenkov and Medvedev [5] also
discuss the reflected extended-real group D∗H ; it is not among these six and is not included in the
theorem. Thus the theorem concerns exactly the six groups displayed above.
   Section 2 recalls the order and normal-subgroup facts needed for the six groups. Section 3
constructs the automorphism. Section 4 identifies the action on the least component, and Section 5
proves that no element of an ambient Dlab group induces this automorphism by conjugation.

                 2. The six Dlab groups and the least action component
   We use the usual order topology on the unit interval or on R = {−∞} ∪ R ∪ {+∞}, according to
the group. Thus every action component considered below is an open interval in a separable linear
continuum; if one of its endpoints is infinite, the other arguments are understood in the extended
order. For a subgroup K ≤ R×     >0 , write DK ([0, 1]) for Dlab’s compact-support group of increasing
locally right K-linear homeomorphisms of [0, 1]. For a nonidentity element x of a linearly ordered
group, write sgn(x) = + if x > 1 and sgn(x) = − if x < 1.
   We shall use two facts from the definitions of these Dlab groups. For a nonidentity element,
the first breakpoint means the first point of its breakpoint sequence, equivalently the left endpoint
of its first support component. First, the breakpoint sequence of every element of these groups is
well ordered from left to right; hence the nonempty family of its support components has a least
member. Second, at every finite fixed point an element is affine on some right neighborhood, with
slope in the prescribed subgroup of R×   >0 . These properties follow from the definitions in [1, Sec. 2]
and [5, Sec. 1–2].
   Dlab [1, Theorems 4.1 and 4.3] proved that DK ([0, 1]) is algebraically simple and that its linear
orders correspond to the linear orders of K. For rank-one K, there are exactly two such orders, and
the sign of a nonidentity element is determined by whether the right slope at its first breakpoint is
greater or less than 1 in the chosen order of K. The analogous two-order statements for the one-sided
interval and extended-real groups are proved in [5, Theorems 1.1 and 2.1]. For the compact-support
group DH on the extended real line, the same first-breakpoint description is given in [3, Sec. 1].
Proposition 2.1. Let H ≤ R×
                          >0 have rank one, let A be one of
                       DH (I),    DH∗ (I),    D∗H (I),   DH (I),    DH ,   DH∗ ,
and let P ≤ A be perfect. For every linear order on A, there is a normal subgroup N ◁ A containing
P such that the order induced on N determines the sign of every nonidentity element of P from
its leftmost support component and the right slope at the first breakpoint of that component. More
precisely:
                             ORDER AUTOMORPHISM OF A DLAB GROUP                                      3


     (i) for A = DH (I), take N = DH (I). This is the compact-support group; by [1, Theorem 4.1],
         for rank-one H its two linear orders are exactly the two first-breakpoint orders;
    (ii) for A = DH∗ (I), take N = DH∗ (I); the proof of [5, Theorem 1.1] shows that its two orders
         are exactly the two first-breakpoint orders;
   (iii) for A = D∗H (I), the normal-structure theorem in [1, Theorem 4.3] gives D∗H (I)/DH (I) ∼ =
         H. Hence perfection gives P ≤ DH (I), and [1, Theorem 4.1] applies to the restricted order;
   (iv) for A = DH (I), the normal-structure theorem in [1, Theorem 4.3] gives DH (I)/DH∗ (I) ∼   =
         H. Hence P ≤ DH∗ (I), and then [5, Theorem 1.1] applies;
    (v) for A = DH∗ , take N = DH∗ and use [5, Theorem 2.1];
   (vi) for A = DH , take N = DH . This compact-support extended-real group has exactly the two
         first-breakpoint orders by [3, Sec. 1].
In cases (iii) and (iv), the order on the indicated normal subgroup is simply the restriction of the
given order on A. No additional choice of order is made. In case (vi) no passage to a smaller
normal subgroup is needed.
Proof. Only (iii) and (iv) require passing to a proper normal subgroup. The full normal-structure
theorem in [1, Theorem 4.3] gives
                          D∗H (I)/DH (I) ∼
                                         = H,        DH (I)/DH∗ (I) ∼
                                                                    = H.
Since H is abelian, a perfect subgroup has trivial image in either quotient. Thus P lies in the
stated kernel. The remaining assertions are precisely the cited order classifications. In particular,
replacing the order of the rank-one slope group by its inverse reverses the two signs but does not
change the first-breakpoint rule.                                                                  □
  For an interval X, let Homeo+ (X) denote the group of increasing homeomorphisms of X. For
subsets E, F of a linearly ordered set, write E < F if every point of E precedes every point of F .
We shall use the following elementary facts.
Lemma 2.2. Let X be an interval, and let B, C ≤ Homeo+ (X).
    (i) If c ∈ Homeo+ (X) normalizes B, then c preserves Fix(B) and permutes the components of
        X \ Fix(B) in their natural order. Consequently, if those components have a least member,
        c fixes it setwise.
   (ii) If B ≤ C, every action component of B is contained in an action component of C.
  (iii) If J is an action component of B, then a nonempty interval V ⊆ J which is invariant under
        all of B must equal J.
Proof. For (i), if x ∈ Fix(B) and b ∈ B, then b(cx) = c(c−1 bc)x = cx; applying the same argument
to c−1 gives c Fix(B) = Fix(B). An increasing homeomorphism therefore permutes the comple-
mentary components in order, and an order automorphism of a linearly ordered set fixes its least
element. For (ii), Fix(C) ⊆ Fix(B), so each component of the complement of Fix(B) lies in one
component of the complement of Fix(C). For (iii), if V ̸= J, at least one endpoint of V lies in the
interior of J. Every increasing homeomorphism preserving V fixes that endpoint, contrary to the
definition of J.                                                                                 □
Proposition 2.3. Let G = D⟨2⟩ ([0, 1]), let H ≤ R×>0 have rank one, and let e : G ,→ A be an order-
preserving embedding into one of the six groups above. Then the nontrivial action components of
e(G) have a least member J0 . The restriction of e(G) to every nontrivial action component is
faithful, and for each 1 ̸= f ∈ G the leftmost support component of e(f ) lies in J0 ; its first right
slope gives exactly the sign of f .
Proof. The group G is nonabelian simple, hence perfect. Proposition 2.1 places e(G), when neces-
sary, in a normal kernel on which the ambient order has the first-breakpoint description.
4                       TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


   Let F = Fix(e(G)), and let J be a component of the complement of F . The kernel of the
restriction homomorphism G → Homeo+ (J) is normal in G. The action on J is nontrivial by
definition, so simplicity makes this kernel trivial. Thus every nonidentity element of G moves a
point in every action component.
   Fix 1 ̸= b ∈ G. Each action component J therefore contains a support component of e(b): if
x ∈ J is moved by e(b), the support component of e(b) containing x cannot cross an endpoint of J,
since such an endpoint belongs to F . Choose, in each J, the first support component of e(b) lying
in J. If J1 < J2 , the chosen component in J1 precedes the one in J2 . Since the support components
of the element e(b) are well ordered, the action components themselves have a least member J0 .
   Now let 1 ̸= f ∈ G. Faithfulness on J0 implies that e(f ) has support in J0 . No support can occur
to the left of J0 : outside the action components every point is fixed by e(G), and by minimality
there is no earlier action component. Hence the global leftmost support component of e(f ) lies in
J0 . By Proposition 2.1, the ambient sign is determined by the first right slope there, and order
preservation identifies it with the sign of f in G.                                                □
Remark 2.4. The rank-one hypothesis on the ambient slope group is essential for the order classi-
fication used above. No assertion for arbitrary higher-rank slope groups is made here.

                           3. The alternating-slope automorphism
    Set
                                      xn = 2−(n+1)      (n ≥ 0).
Define h : [0, 1] → [0, 1] to be the identity on [1/2, 1]. For each m ≥ 0, prescribe slope 2 on
[x2m+2 , x2m+1 ] and slope 1/2 on [x2m+1 , x2m ], joining the pieces continuously from the right.
Lemma 3.1. The map h is an increasing homeomorphism of [0, 1], it fixes every x2m , and its
support components are
                          Cm = (x2m+2 , x2m )  (m ≥ 0).
In particular Cm+1 < Cm , so the family of support components of h has no least member.
Proof. On the block [x2m+2 , x2m ], the prescribed image length is
                                             1
                       2(x2m+1 − x2m+2 ) + (x2m − x2m+1 ) = x2m − x2m+2 ,
                                             2
using xn+1 = xn /2. Since h(x0 ) = x0 , induction from right to left gives h(x2m ) = x2m for all m.
All slopes are positive, and the fixed points x2m tend to 0, so h is an increasing homeomorphism
fixing both endpoints.
   On the lower half of each block the derivative of h(x) − x is 1, while on the upper half it is −1/2.
The difference vanishes at the two block endpoints and is positive in between. Hence the support
components are exactly the Cm .                                                                      □
Proposition 3.2. The formula
                                           αh (f ) = h−1 f h
defines an order automorphism of G.
Proof. Every f ∈ G is the identity on neighborhoods of 0 and 1. Its support is therefore contained
in a compact subinterval of (0, 1), on which h and h−1 have only finitely many affine pieces, all
with slopes in ⟨2⟩. Hence h−1 f h ∈ G, and the same argument with h−1 gives h−1 Gh = G.
   Conjugation by an increasing homeomorphism carries support components exactly to their in-
verse images:
                                   supp(h−1 f h) = h−1 (supp(f )).
                             ORDER AUTOMORPHISM OF A DLAB GROUP                                       5


Thus it preserves their left-to-right order and cannot create a new support component to the left
of the old first one. Let a be the left endpoint of a support component of f , let a′ = h−1 (a), and
let k be the right slope of f at a. Since a′ > 0, there are c ∈ ⟨2⟩ and ε > 0 such that
                                 h(a′ + t) = a + ct      (0 ≤ t < ε).
After decreasing ε, the right germ of f at a is f (a + s) = a + ks, and the corresponding affine piece
of h−1 has slope c−1 . Therefore
                                        (h−1 f h)(a′ + t) = a′ + kt
for all sufficiently small t > 0. The first breakpoint and its right slope are consequently transported
to a′ with the slope unchanged. Since both Dlab orders on G are determined by that first slope,
αh preserves the chosen order.                                                                       □

                           4. The action on the least component
   Fix an order-preserving embedding e : G ,→ A and the least action component J0 from Proposi-
tion 2.3. For a relatively compact open interval L in (0, 1), written L ⋐ (0, 1), set
                                   G(L) = {g ∈ G : supp(g) ⋐ L}.
After an affine change of coordinates, G(L) is a compact-support Dlab group with slope group ⟨2⟩;
in particular it is nonabelian simple and perfect.
   The restriction of e(G(L)) to any of its nontrivial action components is faithful: the restriction
kernel is normal in the simple group G(L), and the action on such a component is nontrivial.
Moreover, e(G(L)) acts nontrivially somewhere in J0 : choose 1 ̸= f ∈ G(L) and use faithfulness of
e(G) on J0 . Hence e(G(L)) has at least one action component in J0 . Fixing such an f , faithfulness
on every one of these components implies that each contains a support component of e(f ). The
well ordering of the support components of e(f ) therefore gives a least e(G(L))-action component
in J0 , which we denote by K(L).
Lemma 4.1. Let L ⋐ (0, 1), put P = e(G(L)), and let a be the left endpoint of K(L) in the ambient
ordered interval. For 1 ̸= p ∈ P , let λ(p) be the left endpoint of the first support component of p in
K(L). Then λ(p) is the global first breakpoint of p, and
                            λ(p) > a    (1 ̸= p ∈ P ),     inf λ(p) = a.                          (4.1)
                                                          1̸=p∈P

Proof. There is no e(G)-action component to the left of J0 , and points outside the action compo-
nents are fixed by e(G). Inside J0 , there is no P -action component to the left of K(L). Hence
every point preceding K(L) is fixed by P , so the first support component of a nonidentity p ∈ P
occurring in K(L) is its global first support component.
   If a is finite, every element of P fixes a. The right germ at a, meaning the restriction to a
sufficiently small right neighborhood of a, is affine. Taking its slope gives a homomorphism
                                            γa : P −→ H,
where γa (p) is the slope of the right germ at a. Since P is perfect and H is abelian, γa (P ) = 1.
A linear germ of slope 1 through the fixed point a is the identity germ, so each p fixes a right
neighborhood of a, proving λ(p) > a. If a = −∞, then the ambient interval is R. Only the
extended-real groups can occur. Proposition 2.1 places P in DH or DH∗ . By the defining condition
in Zenkov–Medvedev, every element of DH∗ fixes an initial interval (−∞, c] for some finite c,
and DH ≤ DH∗ ; see [5, Sec. 2]. Thus every nonidentity p ∈ P has a finite first breakpoint, so
λ(p) > −∞ = a.
   Finally, if the infimum in (4.1) were c > a, then every element of P would fix the nonempty
initial interval (a, c) of K(L), contrary to the definition of an action component. Thus the infimum
is a.                                                                                              □
6                       TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


Lemma 4.2. If L, M ⋐ (0, 1) and L < M , then K(L) and K(M ) are disjoint.
Proof. Put P = e(G(L)) and Q = e(G(M )). These groups commute. Hence every element of Q
normalizes P , and Lemma 2.2(i) shows that it fixes the least P -component K(L) setwise. Similarly,
P fixes K(M ) setwise.
  Suppose the two intervals meet. Their intersection is a nonempty interval invariant under both
groups. Lemma 2.2(iii), first for P and then for Q, gives
                                        K(L) = K(M ) =: K.
Let a be its left endpoint. For 1 ̸= p ∈ P and 1 ̸= q ∈ Q, Lemma 4.1 gives first breakpoints
λ(p), λ(q) > a and
                                    inf λ(p) = a = inf λ(q).                           (4.2)
                                    1̸=p∈P             1̸=q∈Q
   Choose p = e(f ) ̸= 1 in P and q = e(g) ̸= 1 in Q. Since L < M , the source element f g n has
the same sign as f for every n ∈ Z: for n ̸= 0, its first support component lies in L, and n = 0 is
immediate. Thus
                                     sgn(pq n ) = sgn(p)     (n ∈ Z).                              (4.3)
We claim that λ(p) < λ(q). If λ(q) < λ(p), then p is the identity on a right neighborhood of λ(q),
so the first germ of pq n there is exactly the first germ of q n . The elements q and q −1 have opposite
signs; taking n = 1 or −1 contradicts (4.3).
   It remains to exclude λ(p) = λ(q) = c. Let s ̸= 1 and t ̸= 1 be the right slopes of the first germs
of p and q at c. On a common sufficiently small right neighborhood of c, both maps are linear and
fix c, so the first germ of pq n has slope stn . The set {stn : n ∈ Z} has members on both sides of 1:
if t > 1, then stn → ∞ as n → +∞ and stn → 0 as n → −∞, and the case t < 1 is reversed. At
most one integer can satisfy stn = 1, so we may choose n on the side opposite to s with stn ̸= 1.
For this n there is no cancellation of the first germ: c remains the first breakpoint of pq n , and
Proposition 2.3 then gives pq n a sign opposite to that of p. This again contradicts (4.3). Passing to
the other rank-one order reverses both slope comparisons, so the same conclusion holds for either
Dlab order. Consequently
                              λ(p) < λ(q)      (1 ̸= p ∈ P, 1 ̸= q ∈ Q).                           (4.4)
Fixing 1 ̸= p0 ∈ P , equation (4.4) gives λ(q) > λ(p0 ) > a for every 1 ̸= q ∈ Q, contradicting the
second equality in (4.2). Hence K(L) and K(M ) are disjoint.                                     □
Lemma 4.3. For relatively compact open intervals L, M ⋐ (0, 1) the following hold.
    (i) If L ⊂ M , then K(L) ⊂ K(M ).
   (ii) If L < M , then K(L) < K(M ).
  (iii) For every g ∈ G, e(g)K(L) = K(g(L)).
Moreover,                              [
                                            K(L) = J0 .
                                          L⋐(0,1)

Proof. Suppose L ⊂ M . Since G(L) ≤ G(M ), Lemma 2.2(ii) says that every e(G(L))-action
component is contained in an e(G(M ))-action component. The restriction of e(G(M )) to K(M ) is
faithful. Hence any fixed nonidentity element of e(G(L)) acts nontrivially on K(M ). Thus some
point of K(M ) is moved by e(G(L)). The e(G(L))-action component containing that point lies
entirely in K(M ), because the endpoints of K(M ) are fixed by e(G(M )), hence by e(G(L)). Denote
this component by C. If an e(G(L))-component preceded K(M ), Lemma 2.2(ii) would place it in
an e(G(M ))-component preceding K(M ), impossible. Therefore C is the least e(G(L))-component,
namely K(L). This proves (i).
   Now let L < M . Lemma 4.2 makes K(L) and K(M ) disjoint. Choose 1 ̸= f ∈ G(L) positive
and 1 ̸= g ∈ G(M ) negative. Then f g > 1, because its first source support component is the one
                              ORDER AUTOMORPHISM OF A DLAB GROUP                                        7


in L. If K(M ) < K(L), minimality of K(L) implies that e(G(L)) fixes K(M ) pointwise. On the
other hand, faithfulness of e(G(M )) on K(M ) makes the first support component of e(g) in J0
lie in K(M ). Hence the first support component of e(f g) in J0 is that of e(g), so Proposition 2.3
makes e(f g) < 1, contradicting order preservation. Thus K(L) < K(M ), proving (ii).
   For (iii), conjugation gives gG(L)g −1 = G(g(L)), and g(L) ⋐ (0, 1) because g is a homeomor-
phism of (0, 1). Thus conjugation by e(g) sends e(G(L)) onto e(G(g(L))), and e(g) sends their
action components order-preservingly onto one another. Indeed, if J is a component of the comple-
ment of Fix(e(G(L))), then e(g)J is a component of the complement of Fix(e(G(g(L)))), because
conjugation by e(g) carries the two fixed sets onto one another. Since e(g) is increasing, this corre-
spondence preserves the order of components and therefore sends the least component to the least
component. Hence
               S      e(g)K(L) = K(g(L)).
   Put U = L K(L). It is nonempty and open. If y, z ∈ U , choose L, M with y ∈ K(L) and
z ∈ K(M ), and then choose N ⋐ (0, 1) containing L ∪ M . Part (i) gives K(L), K(M ) ⊂ K(N ), so
the interval between y and z lies in K(N ). Thus U is an interval. Part (iii) makes it e(G)-invariant.
If U ̸= J0 , then because both are nonempty open intervals and U ⊂ J0 , at least one endpoint of U
is a finite point in the interior of J0 . Every increasing homeomorphism preserving U setwise fixes
that endpoint, producing a common fixed point of e(G) in J0 , a contradiction. Hence U = J0 . □
  We shall also use the following elementary transitivity fact.
Lemma 4.4. The group G acts transitively on (0, 1).
Proof. It is enough to move a point a sufficiently small distance to the right, since finitely many
such moves and their inverses connect any two points of (0, 1). Let x < y satisfy
                                        y < 2x,      2y − x < 1.
Put a = 2x − y and d = 2y − x. Define an increasing piecewise linear homeomorphism to be the
identity off [a, d], to have slope 2 on [a, x], and slope 1/2 on [x, d]. The two pieces join continuously
and return to the identity at d, while
                                       f (x) = a + 2(x − a) = y.
Thus f ∈ G and sends x to y. For arbitrary 0 < x < y < 1, choose a partition x = t0 < t1 < · · · <
tn = y with mesh smaller than min{x/2, (1 − y)/2}. Then ti+1 < 2ti and 2ti+1 − ti < 1 for every i,
so the preceding construction sends ti to ti+1 . Composing these finitely many bumps sends x to y;
leftward motion follows by inversion.                                                            □
   For an open interval I in the ambient ordered interval, write ℓ− (I) and ℓ+ (I) for its left and
right endpoints. Fix x ∈ (0, 1) and define
              ax = sup{ℓ+ (K(L)) : L ⋐ (0, x)},         bx = inf{ℓ− (K(R)) : R ⋐ (x, 1)}.          (4.5)
Both sets are nonempty. By Lemma 4.3(ii), every interval K(L) used in the first set lies strictly to
the left of every interval K(R) used in the second. Fix L0 ⋐ (0, x) and R0 ⋐ (x, 1). Then
                        ℓ+ (K(L)) ≤ ℓ− (K(R0 )),        ℓ− (K(R)) ≥ ℓ+ (K(L0 ))
for all admissible L, R. The two displayed bounding points are finite: K(L0 ) < K(R0 ) are disjoint
open intervals inside J0 , so their adjacent endpoints are finite real points of the ambient interval.
Completeness of R therefore gives finite ax , bx ∈ J0 with ax ≤ bx . Put
                                          Fx = [ax , bx ] ⊂ J0 .
Lemma 4.5. If x < z, then Fx < Fz . Moreover
                                     e(g)Fx = Fg(x)        (g ∈ G).                                (4.6)
Consequently every Fx is a singleton.
8                        TING GONG, YONG YANG, AND MICHAEL RUOFAN ZENG


Proof. Choose M ⋐ (0, 1) with x < M < z. Since M occurs on the right of x and on the left of z,
definition (4.5) gives
                                  bx ≤ ℓ− (K(M )) < ℓ+ (K(M )) ≤ az .
Thus Fx < Fz .
   For the second assertion, g bijects the relatively compact intervals in (0, x) with those in (0, g(x)),
and similarly on the right. By Lemma 4.3(iii), e(g)K(L) = K(g(L)). An increasing homeomorphism
of an interval preserves endpoints and existing suprema and infima. Applying e(g) to the two cuts
in (4.5) therefore gives e(g)ax = ag(x) and e(g)bx = bg(x) , proving (4.6).
   The intervals Fx are pairwise disjoint. Suppose one, say Fx , is nondegenerate. Its interior is then
a nonempty open interval. By Lemma 4.4 and (4.6), every Fz is the image of Fx under an increasing
homeomorphism and is therefore nondegenerate. This yields uncountably many pairwise disjoint
nonempty open subintervals of J0 . But J0 , being an interval in R, has a countable dense subset,
and each member of a pairwise disjoint family of nonempty open intervals contains a distinct point
of that subset. This is impossible. Hence every Fx is a singleton.                                      □
    Let φ(x) be the unique point of Fx .
Proposition 4.6. The map
                                        φ : (0, 1) −→ J0
is an increasing homeomorphism satisfying
                               φ(gx) = e(g)φ(x)       (g ∈ G, x ∈ (0, 1)).                          (4.7)
Equivalently, with π = φ−1 ,
                                     e(g)|J0 = π −1 gπ      (g ∈ G).
Proof. Lemma 4.5 shows that x < z implies φ(x) < φ(z), so φ is strictly increasing, and (4.6) gives
(4.7).
   A monotone map between real intervals can fail to be continuous only by a jump. Suppose,
for example, that φ has a nonempty left jump interval at x. For any g ∈ G, continuity and
monotonicity of the already given homeomorphism e(g), together with (4.7), carry that jump
interval homeomorphically to the left jump interval at g(x). The same holds for right jumps. By
Lemma 4.4, one jump would therefore produce uncountably many pairwise disjoint nonempty open
intervals in J0 , contradicting the separability argument used in Lemma 4.5. Thus φ is continuous.
   A continuous strictly increasing map has interval image. Write
                                    α = lim φ(x),        β = lim φ(x)
                                           x↓0               x↑1

in the extended closure of J0 . Then φ((0, 1)) = (α, β), an open subinterval of J0 . Equation (4.7)
makes this image e(G)-invariant. If it were proper, one of α, β would be a finite point in the interior
of J0 . Every increasing homeomorphism preserving (α, β) setwise fixes such an endpoint, giving a
common fixed point of e(G) inside the action component J0 , a contradiction. Therefore the image
is all of J0 . A continuous strictly increasing bijection between intervals is a homeomorphism, and
(4.7) gives the displayed conjugacy.                                                                 □

                                    5. Excluding conjugation
Lemma 5.1. The centralizer of the standard action of G in Homeo+ ((0, 1)) is trivial.
Proof. Let c commute with G, and suppose c(x) ̸= x. Replacing c by c−1 if necessary, assume
x < c(x). Choose x < y < c(x). By continuity of c, a sufficiently small relatively compact open
interval U ∋ x satisfies sup U < inf c(U ), hence U ∩ c(U ) = ∅. The two-slope bump construction
from Lemma 4.4, with all breakpoints in U , gives 1 ̸= g ∈ G with supp(g) ⋐ U . Commutation
gives
                               c(supp(g)) = supp(cgc−1 ) = supp(g),
                              ORDER AUTOMORPHISM OF A DLAB GROUP                                        9


while the two sides lie in the disjoint intervals c(U ) and U , a contradiction. Hence c = 1.          □

Proposition 5.2. No u ∈ A induces αh on e(G) by conjugation.

Proof. Suppose that
                                  e(αh (f )) = u−1 e(f )u        (f ∈ G).                          (5.1)
Then u normalizes e(G). Lemma 2.2(i) says that u permutes the action components of e(G) in
order, so it fixes the least one J0 setwise.
  Let π : J0 → (0, 1) be the increasing conjugacy from Proposition 4.6, and put

                                            v = π(u|J0 )π −1 .

Transporting (5.1) to (0, 1) gives

                                     v −1 f v = h−1 f h     (f ∈ G).

Thus vh−1 centralizes the standard action of G, and Lemma 5.1 yields v = h.
   By Lemma 3.1, the support components of h are Cm = (x2m+2 , x2m ), with Cm+1 < Cm and no
least member. Therefore
                                            Dm = π −1 (Cm )
is a component of supp(u)∩J0 . Its two endpoints π −1 (x2m+2 ) and π −1 (x2m ) are finite interior points
of J0 fixed by u, because u|J0 = π −1 hπ. Hence no connected component of the open set supp(u)
can cross either endpoint of Dm . Thus every Dm is a full support component of u, not merely a
component of its restriction to J0 . Since Dm+1 < Dm for all m, these support components form a
nonempty family with no least member, contradicting the well-ordering of support components of
an element of a Dlab group. This proves the proposition.                                               □

Proof of Theorem 1.1. By Proposition 3.2, αh is an order automorphism of G. Proposition 4.6
identifies the action of e(G) on J0 with the standard action of G, and Proposition 5.2 shows that
no element of any of the six groups induces αh by conjugation.                                 □
